cards.title: Giant trees pull water hundreds of feet upward using negative pressure
cards.body: Capillary action can only lift water about three feet, yet giant redwoods drink from soil over three hundred feet below their canopies. They manage this without mechanical pumps. As water evaporates from microscopic pores in leaves, hydrogen bonds between water molecules drag upward in an unbroken chain. This creates enormous negative pressure—over twenty atmospheres of tension—literally pulling liquid water up through the xylem like a rope.

sources.title: Water Uptake and Transport in Vascular Plants

cards.title: Airplane wings do not generate lift by forcing air to meet up
cards.body: A popular textbook explanation claims air flowing over a wing's curved top must reach the trailing edge at the exact same time as air flowing underneath. Because the upper path is longer, air supposedly accelerates, lowering pressure. But wind-tunnel tests prove air particles never meet up: air flowing over the top arrives much faster than the air below. Lift is fundamentally generated by deflecting massive amounts of air downward, obeying Newton's laws of motion.

cards.title: The sky is blue because sunlight scatters across gas molecules
cards.body: Sunlight looks white, but it contains all the colors of the rainbow. When sunlight enters Earth's atmosphere, it collides with nitrogen and oxygen molecules. Shorter wavelengths of light scatter much more intensely than longer ones—a process called Rayleigh scattering. Because blue and violet light have the shortest visible wavelengths, they scatter in every direction across the sky. Human eyes are far more sensitive to blue than violet, painting the daytime sky blue.

cards.title: Your nerve impulses travel much slower than the speed of light
cards.body: Because we describe nerve impulses as electrical signals, many assume they zip through the body at near the speed of light. In reality, nerve conduction relies on ions physically diffusing across cell membranes. The fastest myelinated human nerves transmit signals at roughly one hundred twenty meters per second—about two hundred seventy miles per hour. Slower pain signals crawl at less than two meters per second, which is why a stubbed toe registers dull throbbing only after a distinct delay.

cards.title: Pressure alone does not melt ice beneath an ice skater's blade
cards.body: Generations of science students learned that ice skates glide because the skater's body weight exerts crushing pressure, lowering the melting point and creating a thin film of water. In truth, human weight only drops ice's melting point by a fraction of a degree Celsius—nowhere near enough on a freezing rink. Ice is naturally slippery because its outermost surface possesses a microscopic, disordered, liquid-like layer even tens of degrees below freezing, aided by friction.

sources.title: Focus: Friction of Ice Is Driven by Water-Like Layer

quizzes.question: How do tall trees transport water from the soil up hundreds of feet into their canopies?
options: Through immense negative pressure generated as water evaporates from leaves
By actively pumping water upward using microscopic muscular valves
Exclusively through capillary action inside narrow xylem vessels
By absorbing moisture strictly through needles directly from low-hanging clouds
quizzes.explanation: Transpiration pulls unbroken chains of water molecules upward under tens of atmospheres of negative pressure.

quizzes.question: What does wind-tunnel testing reveal about air flowing over an airplane wing?
options: Air over the curved top reaches the trailing edge much faster than air below
Air over the top and bottom meet up at the exact same instant
Air below the wing accelerates to twice the speed of air on top
Air does not move relative to the wing surface during steady flight
quizzes.explanation: Air traveling over the curved upper surface speeds up so significantly that it arrives far ahead of the air beneath.

quizzes.question: Why does Rayleigh scattering cause the daytime sky to look blue instead of red?
options: Shorter visible wavelengths like blue scatter much more easily off gas molecules
Atmospheric nitrogen chemically absorbs red light and re-emits blue light
Sunlight contains only blue and violet light when leaving the Sun
Ocean water reflects blue light upward to color the surrounding atmosphere
quizzes.explanation: Rayleigh scattering intensity is inversely proportional to the fourth power of wavelength, scattering blue light far more than red.

quizzes.question: Roughly how fast do signals travel along the fastest human nerve fibers?
options: Around 120 meters per second
Around 300,000 kilometers per second
Roughly 5 miles per hour
At the speed of light in a vacuum
quizzes.explanation: Because nerve impulses rely on physical ion movement across membranes, they top out at roughly 120 m/s (~270 mph).

quizzes.question: Why is ice naturally slippery even before an ice skate exerts pressure on it?
options: Its outermost surface has a microscopic, disordered liquid-like layer
A layer of compressed air constantly outgasses from inside the ice
Ice molecules actively repel all metals and synthetic plastics
Sublimation instantly turns the top ice layer into high-pressure steam
quizzes.explanation: Ice naturally maintains a quasi-liquid surface layer well below freezing, which lubricates contact even without blade pressure.

guesses.prompt: What is the maximum speed (in meters per second) of nerve impulses along the fastest human nerve fibers?
guesses.explanation: The fastest myelinated nerves transmit at roughly 120 m/s (~270 mph), far slower than the speed of light.

misconceptions.claim: Air traveling over the curved top of an airplane wing must reach the back edge at the same time as air underneath.
misconceptions.explanation: Wind-tunnel experiments prove the upper air arrives at the trailing edge significantly earlier than the lower air.

misconceptions.claim: Violet light scatters even more strongly in Earth's atmosphere than blue light.
misconceptions.explanation: Violet light has a shorter wavelength and scatters more than blue, but our eyes are far more sensitive to blue cones.

misconceptions.claim: Ice skates glide smoothly because the skater's body weight creates enough pressure to melt the ice into liquid water.
misconceptions.explanation: Skater pressure only lowers ice's melting point by a fraction of a degree; ice is slippery due to an inherent quasi-liquid surface layer.
